analysis.one_liner: Abolishes OSHA, the federal agency that sets and enforces workplace safety rules.
analysis.headline: The bill to abolish OSHA never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Education and Workforce Committee when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 and shut down OSHA, the Department of Labor agency that writes and enforces workplace safety and health standards, including rules on hazards, inspections, and employer citations for violations. Without it, no federal agency would set or enforce those standards. The bill attracted one cosponsor, was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, and never moved further.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers, especially those in hazardous industries, gain if the bill passes: no federal inspections, no citations, no penalties for safety violations, and lower compliance costs. Businesses that spend money meeting OSHA standards save those costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers facing safety inspections and fines

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 in its entirety and abolishes OSHA, eliminating federal workplace safety standards, inspections, citations, and penalties [S2] [S3].
Removes compliance costs for employers who currently spend money meeting OSHA standards, since no federal agency would set or enforce replacement rules [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Workers in dangerous jobs — construction, manufacturing, meatpacking, warehousing — would bear the cost, since no federal agency would set enforceable safety standards or inspect workplaces, and injuries, illnesses, and deaths that OSHA rules and penalties deter would rise. Their families and taxpayers (through workers' compensation, disability, and emergency care) would absorb part of that cost.

drawbacks.text: OSHA compliance is a real expense for employers, and small businesses in particular have long argued some standards are costly relative to the risk they address [S2].
The bill offers no replacement: it simply repeals the 1970 Act and abolishes the agency, leaving no federal body to investigate workplace deaths, set hazard limits, or require safety equipment [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings to businesses are real but small compared with what workers would lose: OSHA's standards and penalties are the main federal backstop against unsafe workplaces, and the bill replaces that system with nothing. Most employer costs from safety rules are costs of preventing injuries and deaths, so eliminating them shifts those risks onto workers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee took no further action on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Biggs introduced the bill on January 9, 2023, the opening days of the 118th Congress [S1] [S5].
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day [S5].
It attracted a single cosponsor, one of 224 House Republicans [S4].
The committee held no markup, hearing, or floor vote on the bill, and it died there when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers are better off because the bill died: OSHA's safety standards, inspections, and employer penalties remain in place. The employers who would have shed compliance costs and enforcement risk did not get that outcome.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers, who kept federal safety protections

for.name: Rep. Andy Biggs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the OSH Act and abolish OSHA

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 9, 2023 and took no further action — no markup, no hearing on the bill, no report to the floor

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Republican sponsor and one Republican cosponsor, and no other member of either party signed on, so no party took a position through a vote.

industries.industry: Employers in hazardous industries (construction, manufacturing, warehousing, meatpacking)
industries.note: Had the bill passed, these employers would have been freed from federal safety inspections, citations, and penalties, cutting compliance costs. The savings come at workers' expense, since no agency would enforce safety standards.

industries.industry: State OSHA programs and workplace safety consultants/trainers
industries.note: Repealing the 1970 Act would end the federal framework that underwrites state safety plans and creates demand for private safety compliance services; some of that demand could persist or shift, but the bill's text provides no replacement structure [S3].
